Argentière — Lateglacial and Younger Dryas temperature from dated landforms, 13.6–9.0 ka¶

Goal. Reconstruct the temperature of the Allerød, the Younger Dryas and the Preboreal (13.6 → 9.0 ka BP) from the dated moraines and exposure ages of Argentière glacier and its neighbours in the upper Arve (Mer de Glace with Talèfre), Mont Blanc massif. The control is the temperature at 2000 m, T(t): 24 nodes every 200 yr, linear in between. Precipitation follows it (Clausius–Clapeyron, 7 %/°C); everything else in the mass balance and the ice flow is fixed, and section 11 measures what those fixed choices do to T(t).

Current strategy
window 13.6 → 9.0 ka BP only; the late-Holocene window was dropped
grid 100 m (250 × 250 cells)
mass balance literature climate: P 1.8 m/yr, T_s 9.4 °C, degree-day factor 10 mm/K/d, present temperature fitted to the 2012–2021 geodetic balance (section 9)
temperature kept inside a literature envelope (section 9)
landforms scored along each valley's flowline, grouped robust data term (section 7.1)
gradient frozen-velocity, first-order-upwind adjoint, capped (sections 7.4, 8)
result results/argentiere_lg_100m_phys (section 10)
uncertainty sensitivity to every fixed parameter, data-only uncertainty per period (section 11)

Data (built by tools/prepare_argentiere_data.py, described in data/Argentiere/README.md):

  • AlpIce-1 (Kamleitner et al. 2026): ¹⁰Be-dated lateral and frontal moraines (Lognan, La Joux, Talèfre), bedrock and erratic exposure ages (Lognan, Mer de Glace transects, Aiguilles Rouges).
  • LIA extent and ice surface (Reinthaler & Paul 2025): the starting glacier, and the calibration of the lateral-moraine operator.
  • Present: Argentière 2012 and 2021 thickness and the 2012–2021 stake balance, for the mass-balance calibration.

Reading guide. Sections 1, 9, 10 and 11 are the current strategy. Sections 2–8 record how it was reached, with earlier 200 m runs that are now in results_archive/; their figures are the saved outputs, and cells that read deleted runs (section 8) no longer re-run.

1. The data on the model grid¶

One 100 m grid covers the whole upper Arve (250 × 250 cells, 25 × 25 km). Green shows where ice may grow: the upper Arve basin above the Mer de Glace confluence, plus 8 km down the Arve. (The cyan outline is a tighter Holocene mask that the Lateglacial runs do not use.) The symbols are the Lateglacial constraints inside the basin. The hillshade is lit from the south.

Two corrections were needed before any of this lined up (details in the data README):

  • the Argentière radar/DEM products are 52 m above AW3D30 and the AlpIce-1 sample elevations on ice-free ground — an ellipsoidal vs orthometric datum — so a fitted plane is removed from them;
  • the lateral-moraine operator steps downslope from the crest instead of toward the nearest modern ice, because the Lateglacial ice margins at La Joux are kilometres from any ice today. Its offset, bias and σ are calibrated on the one dated LIA lateral moraine (Talèfre T4) against the LIA surface.

The moraines themselves pass a positional check: the DEM at each dated boulder agrees with the boulder's recorded elevation to within ±25 m.

2. Calibrating the mass balance on the 2012–2021 stakes¶

Superseded by the literature climate of section 9; kept because it shows why the stakes alone cannot fix the precipitation.

The PDD model has three free climate numbers — temperature, precipitation and melt factor — and the 25 Argentière stakes (2365–2977 m, mostly ablation zone) only constrain two of them: the ELA and the balance gradient. Temperature and precipitation trade off almost perfectly along that valley. So the temperature is pinned from outside: 1.0 °C at 2000 m for 2012–2021 (Chamonix, 1042 m, ≈7.5 °C, extrapolated with the model's own 7 °C/km). The stakes then give the melt factor and the precipitation.

Stake altitudes are orthometric (they sit 52 m below the raw 2021 DEM), so no datum shift is needed here.

In [4]:
from core.smb import update_smb_PDD
st = pd.read_csv("data/Argentiere/sources/present/SMB_argentiere_2012-2021_utm32N.csv")
z = torch.tensor(st.Alt.values, dtype=torch.float64); b = st.iloc[:, 3].values
model = lambda T, P, mf: update_smb_PDD(z, P, torch.tensor(T, dtype=torch.float64), 10.0,
                                        melt_factor=mf, z_ref=2000.0).numpy() * 0.91   # -> m w.e.
T_PIN = 1.0
grid = [(np.sqrt(np.mean((model(T_PIN, P, mf) - b) ** 2)), mf, P)
        for mf in np.arange(0.15, 0.40, 0.01) for P in np.arange(1.0, 8.01, 0.1)]
rmse, MF, PREC = min(grid)
print(f"T(2000 m) pinned at {T_PIN} C -> melt factor {MF:.2f} m w.e./(C month), precipitation {PREC:.1f} m/yr, rmse {rmse:.2f} m w.e.")

zz = np.linspace(2300, 3100, 50)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
ax[0].scatter(b, st.Alt, c="k", s=12, label="stakes 2012-2021")
for T in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5):
    mf, P = min(((np.sqrt(np.mean((model(T, P, mf) - b) ** 2)), mf, P) for mf in np.arange(0.15, 0.40, 0.01)
                 for P in np.arange(1.0, 8.01, 0.1)))[1:]
    s = update_smb_PDD(torch.tensor(zz), P, torch.tensor(T, dtype=torch.float64), 10.0, melt_factor=mf, z_ref=2000.0).numpy() * 0.91
    ax[0].plot(s, zz, label=f"T={T}: mf {mf:.2f}, P {P:.1f}")
ax[0].axvline(0, c="grey", lw=.5); ax[0].set_xlabel("SMB (m w.e./yr)"); ax[0].set_ylabel("elevation (m)"); ax[0].legend(fontsize=8)
ax[0].set_title("equally good fits: the stakes cannot separate T from P")
Ts = np.arange(-1, 3.01, 0.25)
best = [min(((np.sqrt(np.mean((model(T, P, mf) - b) ** 2)), P) for mf in np.arange(0.15, 0.40, 0.02)
             for P in np.arange(1.0, 9.01, 0.2))) for T in Ts]
ax[1].plot(Ts, [p for _, p in best], "o-"); ax[1].set_xlabel("pinned T(2000 m), C"); ax[1].set_ylabel("best precipitation (m/yr)")
ax2 = ax[1].twinx(); ax2.plot(Ts, [r for r, _ in best], "s--", c="C1"); ax2.set_ylabel("rmse (m w.e.)", color="C1")
ax[1].set_title("the T-P trade-off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

T(2000 m) pinned at 1.0 C -> melt factor 0.26 m w.e./(C month), precipitation 4.7 m/yr, rmse 0.41 m w.e.

An independent check on the pin: the geodetic balance. The stakes say nothing about the accumulation area, but the 2012→2021 thickness change does: Argentière lost 0.104 km³ of ice over 16 km², −0.61 m w.e./yr. For each pinned temperature, the best stake fit implies a glacier-wide balance on the 2012–2021 surface — which pins are compatible with the geodetic number?

In [5]:
nc = netCDF4.Dataset(f"data/Argentiere/argentiere_100m.nc")
bed100 = np.asarray(nc["topg"][:]); t12 = np.asarray(nc["thk_2012"][:]); t21 = np.asarray(nc["thk_2021"][:])
m12 = np.asarray(nc["argentiere_2012"][:]) > 0.5; nc.close()
geod = (t21 - t12)[m12].sum() / m12.sum() / 9.0 * 0.85          # 850 kg/m3 volume-to-mass
zs = torch.tensor((bed100 + 0.5 * (t12 + t21))[m12], dtype=torch.float64)
gw = []
for T, (r, P) in zip(Ts, best):
    mf = min(((np.sqrt(np.mean((model(T, P, mf) - b) ** 2)), mf) for mf in np.arange(0.15, 0.40, 0.01)))[1]
    gw.append(float((update_smb_PDD(zs, P, torch.tensor(T, dtype=torch.float64), 10.0, melt_factor=mf, z_ref=2000.0).numpy() * 0.91).mean()))
plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3.2)); plt.plot(Ts, gw, "o-", label="model, best stake fit")
plt.axhline(geod, c="k", ls="--", label=f"geodetic 2012-2021: {geod:.2f}")
plt.xlabel("pinned T(2000 m), C"); plt.ylabel("glacier-wide SMB (m w.e./yr)"); plt.legend(fontsize=8); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Pins below about 0.5 °C give a glacier-wide balance that is too negative; from 1 °C up the model sits within ~0.05 m w.e./yr of the geodetic value. The station-based pin of 1.0 °C is therefore consistent with the volume change as well as with the stakes.

The fit is flat along the trade-off line — rmse barely changes from −1 to +3 °C — which is why the temperature has to be pinned. This choice sets the absolute level of every temperature below; anomalies relative to 2012–2021 are much less sensitive to it than absolute values. The runs use melt_factor = 0.26, precip = 4.7 m/yr (BASE in tools/run_argentiere_inversion.py); 4.7 m/yr is an effective number for the whole basin, including avalanche and wind input to the accumulation area.

Precipitation follows temperature (Clausius–Clapeyron). Only temperature is inverted. Precipitation is tied to it at 7 % per °C, P(t) = 4.7 · 1.07^(T(t) − 1.0) m/yr, so 4.7 m/yr is the value at the 2012–2021 temperature. A Younger Dryas 3 °C colder than today then gets 18 % less precipitation, not the same amount.

3. The model and what changed in the code¶

Same IGM-emulator forward model as the Aletsch notebooks. Running it for thousands of years needed four changes, all opt-in so the Aletsch experiments are untouched:

change where why
fixed temperature datum z_ref core/climate.py, core/smb.py, --z_ref the old datum, min(ice surface), moves whenever the lowest cell gains or loses ice — at La Joux that is the whole Lateglacial
smb_freq + linear control interpolation core/glacier.py, --smb_freq with 100–200 yr control nodes the SMB used to be refreshed only once per node; now it follows the surface every 10 yr
two-level checkpointing chunk_steps core/glacier.py, --chunk_steps memory independent of run length (needed at 100 m; tested to give identical gradients)
moraine / exposure operators core/moraine_obs.py each landform scored at the best time inside its age uncertainty (soft minimum over snapshots), bedrock ages as one-sided "ice-free after" constraints
Clausius–Clapeyron precipitation precip_cc core/glacier.py, --precip_cc precipitation scales with the control temperature, so only temperature is inverted
compiled transport core/forward_schemes/igm_emulator_step.py, use_compiled_transport torch.compile of the flux limiter and the emulator network: 2.8× faster forward + backward, gradients equal to 1e-4

Numerics of the current runs: 100 m grid, CFL 0.3, depth-averaged speed capped at 600 m/yr (only icefall cells reach it, section 7.3), SMB updated every 10 yr, two-level checkpointing in blocks of 300 steps. The gradient is the frozen-velocity, first-order-upwind adjoint (--no_emulator_grad --adjoint_slope godunov, sections 7.4 and 8) with the thickness adjoint capped at 0.05 (--adjoint_clip). One iteration (forward and backward) takes about 33 min on an RTX 4090; a forward run alone takes about 9 min.

4. First look: constant-temperature scans¶

Before any gradient, run the window at a handful of constant temperatures and ask, for every dated landform, which temperature fits it best. That is a cheap, model-based reconstruction in its own right, and it gives the inversion its starting point.

(python tools/run_argentiere_inversion.py --window lg --scan 0 -1 -2 -3 -4, plus --scan 0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0 --out_dir results/argentiere_lg_200m_scan_warm once it was clear the Lateglacial optimum is not below 0 °C. 200 m grid and the stake-only climate of section 2. Forward only, ~2.5 min per temperature.)

In [5]:
def load_scan(w):
    # scan.json, plus any extra temperatures run into <results>_scan_*/ (e.g. the warmer lg scan)
    import glob
    with open(f"{RESULTS[w]}/scan.json") as f:
        sc = json.load(f)
    for extra in sorted(glob.glob(f"{RESULTS[w]}_scan_*/scan.json")):
        with open(extra) as f:
            sc["rows"] += json.load(f)["rows"]
    sc["rows"].sort(key=lambda r: r["T"])
    return sc

def best_T(scan, oid):
    T = np.array([r["T"] for r in scan["rows"]]); m = np.array([r["terms"][oid] for r in scan["rows"]])
    i = int(np.argmin(m))
    if 0 < i < len(T) - 1:                       # parabola through the three best points
        a, b_, _ = np.polyfit(T[i - 1:i + 2], m[i - 1:i + 2], 2)
        if a > 0:
            return float(np.clip(-b_ / (2 * a), T[i - 1], T[i + 1])), float(m.min())
    return float(T[i]), float(m.min())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
for w in ("lg",):
    sc = load_scan(w)
    T = [r["T"] for r in sc["rows"]]
    for oid, meta in sc["meta"].items():
        m = [r["terms"][oid] for r in sc["rows"]]
        style = {"lateral": "-", "frontal": "-", "thickness": "--", "extent": "--"}.get(meta["kind"], ":")
        ax.plot(T, m, style, lw=1.2 if style == "-" else 0.7, label=oid if style != ":" else None)
    ax.set_yscale("symlog", linthresh=1); ax.set_xlabel("constant T at 2000 m (C)"); ax.set_ylabel("normalized misfit")
    ax.set_title(f"{w}: misfit of each observation vs temperature"); ax.legend(fontsize=6, ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

5. Gradient inversion: the latest run¶

results/argentiere_lg_100m_phys (launch.sh there). Control: T(t) at 2000 m, 24 nodes every 200 yr from 13.6 to 9.0 ka, linear in between; summed smoothness prior on the second difference. Landforms scored along the valleys with the grouped robust data term (section 7.1). Literature climate and temperature envelope (section 9). 100 m grid, 600 m/yr speed cap (7.3), frozen-velocity upwind adjoint capped at 0.05 (7.4, 8).

Optimizer. Adam, 30 iterations, learning rate on a cosine from 0.05 to 0.01 °C, started from the best iterate of the same inversion at 200 m (results/argentiere_lg_200m_phys). After every step the nodes are projected into the envelope. A step that makes the loss more than 5 % worse than the best so far goes back to the best iterate with half the rate; a non-finite gradient does the same.

  --chunk_steps 300 --init_from results/argentiere_lg_200m_phys/history.json --iters 30 --lr 0.05 --lr_min 0.01

In [2]:
if RUN_HEAVY_CELLS:
    from core.moraine_obs import invert_observations
    from core.utils import device
    torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True
    clim = R.CLIMATES["phys"]
    glacier, geo, obs, node_times, _ = R.build("lg", DX, chunk_steps=300, base=clim, valley=True, max_velbar=600,
                                               adjoint_slope="godunov", emulator_grad=False)
    lo, hi = (torch.tensor(b, dtype=torch.float32, device=device).view(-1, 1) for b in R.temperature_bounds(node_times, clim["T_present"]))
    T = torch.tensor(R.initial_T("results/argentiere_lg_200m_phys/history.json"), device=device).view(-1, 1).requires_grad_(True)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam([T], lr=0.05)
    for i in range(30):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss, data, terms, _ = invert_observations(
            T, glacier, obs, precip_tensor=clim["precip"], T_s=clim["T_s"], melt_factor=clim["melt_factor"],
            dt_snap=R.WINDOWS["lg"]["dt_snap"], reg_lambda=1.0, weighting="groups", reg_sum=True)
        loss.backward(); opt.step()
        with torch.no_grad():
            T.copy_(torch.maximum(torch.minimum(T, hi), lo))
        print(i, float(loss), float(data))
else:
    print("RUN_HEAVY_CELLS is False: loading", RUN100)

5.1 How well is each observation fitted?¶

Misfits are normalized squared residuals: about 1 means "off by one σ". The one-sided constraints read exactly 0 when they are met: a bedrock or erratic sample whose valley-axis ice surface stays below the sample + 10 m at every time after its exposure, or a moraine that no later advance overrode (-preserve). Such a term has no gradient, so it pulls on the temperature only once it is violated. The five samples exposed before 15.6 ka sit hundreds of metres above the modelled ice during the whole run and cannot constrain this window. The metres are read at the best time inside each age window (at the worst time for the one-sided constraints).

6. What the run shows¶

Convergence. 30 iterations (16.8 h) took the loss from 23.66 to 22.74 and the data term from 23.44 to 22.52. The best iterate is the last one and the loss was still falling, by < 0.01 per iteration at the end: a uniform shift of the whole curve would gain only 0.3 more (−0.12 °C, section 11). No step was rejected and no gradient was non-finite. No node touches the literature envelope, so the landforms alone set the curve.

The temperature. Between −5.1 and −5.65 °C at 2000 m from 13.2 to 10.2 ka, with the Younger Dryas mean at −5.54 °C: 4.65 °C below 2012–2021, 2.65 °C below pre-industrial. The coldest node is −5.65 °C at 12.2 ka. From 10.2 ka it warms steadily, to −2.41 °C at 9.0 ka. Precipitation follows: about 0.73 of today's 1.8 m/yr in the Younger Dryas, 0.90 at 9 ka. The Allerød (13.6–13.0 ka) is only 0.1–0.75 °C warmer than the Younger Dryas: the model starts from the LIA glacier at 13.6 ka, and the first centuries mostly spin it up, so these nodes are weakly constrained.

The fit. 19 of 33 constraints have a non-zero misfit (table 5.1).

  • Met: the La Joux J2 frontal moraine (terminus within 0.13 km, but only at 11.9 ka, the old end of its 10.8 ± 1.1 ka window), Lognan L2 (30 m), the Talèfre laterals T1/T2 (within 9 m), and 13 of the 17 bedrock and erratic samples. The modelled stand that builds J2 and the La Joux / Lognan laterals is at 12.2–11.9 ka.
  • Not met, all the same way, too much ice on the sides of the Argentière valley: La Joux J1 (55 m above its crest) and the undated La Joux moraine (78 m), Lognan L1 (77 m) and L3 (62 m), and the bedrock at Mont Blanc Tête de Trélaporte (149 m of ice at 10.6 ka, the largest single term), Aiguille du Moine (96 m at 12.3 ka), the La Joux erratic (83 m) and Lognan Protin 2019-E (46 m).

Diagnosis. The terminus reaches J2, but the valley-side surface is 50–80 m too high at the same time. The inversion cannot fix both with one temperature: a colder climate lengthens the tongue beyond J2, a warmer one moves it off. The excess is therefore a matter of the glacier's shape: ice too thick for its length, which points to the ice flow (flow-law factor, sliding, the speed cap in the Lognan icefall) or to the accumulation pattern rather than to the temperature. Section 11 tests these.

7. Rethinking the comparison with the landforms¶

How the landform comparison of section 5 came about. The first inversion (200 m, stake-only climate, results_archive/argentiere_lg_200m, compared with the latest in section 8) scored each landform by the ice at its own cells (the operators of section 3). Its misfit table said most landforms were fitted, while its maps showed the glacier never got near La Joux. The maps were right. In these valleys the cell operators fail three ways:

  1. A glacier that stops short scores a constant, gradient-free misfit. J1 and the undated La Joux line sit 3–4 km beyond the modelled terminus; their misfits (3.1, 5–8) do not change with anything the inversion can do. The J2 frontal operator returns 0.50 with no ice anywhere (the soft extent indicator is 0.45 on ice-free cells), so the 0.58 of the best run means "no glacier", not "fitted within σ".
  2. Ice that is not the glacier gets scored. A lateral moraine is scored one cell downslope of its crest. That cell often carries ice draped on the valley side or on a nunatak, fed from above. At Talèfre (right panel below) it gives T1 a misfit of 9 and pushes the whole Lateglacial warmer, while on the valley axis the modelled surface is within 15 m of the crest. The Jardin bedrock sample is "violated" by ice on the nunatak itself.
  3. The mean dilutes. Each landform is one of 27 observations, most of them satisfied one-sided constraints that read 0.

Found on the way, unrelated to the operators: igm_emulator_step clamps H at 0 before adding the SMB, so every ice-free cell carries −dt·|SMB| (about −5 m) between steps.

7.1 Valley-referenced operators (--valley)¶

A moraine low in a valley was built by ice that came down that valley. Each valley gets a flowline (core/valley.py): the D8 path along the valley floor of the bed, from the head of the source glacier's valley (climbing into its LIA polygon at junctions) down past its outermost landform, cut before the next glaciated tributary. Every landform cell is referred to its nearest flowline cell — its cross-section on the valley axis. Two quantities are measured there, both differentiable and both defined however far the glacier is:

  • the terminus position L along the flowline: τ·logsumexp(s/τ + log m(H) + Σ log g(H)), a soft maximum of arc length weighted by the soft ice indicator m(H) = 1 − exp(−H/30 m) and by contiguity with the glacier (g: a smoothstep, 1 from 5 m of ice up), τ = 100 m. It is a signed distance along the valley — a one-dimensional SDF — that moves continuously as the snout cell fills, and another glacier's tongue further down the same valley does not count;
  • the ice surface on the valley axis at each landform cell's cross-section.
landform kind asks σ
frontal moraine terminus L = s_moraine at some time in the age window 300 m
lateral moraine lateral_v L ≥ s_moraine, and axis surface = crest + δ 300 m; 60 m
bedrock, erratic icefree_v axis surface ≤ sample + δ after exposure 60 m
a dated moraine survived preserve after its window: L ≤ s_moraine, axis surface ≤ crest + δ same, weight 0.5

δ = +10 m and σ_z = 60 m are the median and scatter of (axis surface − margin surface) along the mapped LIA Argentière.

Weighting (weighting="groups"). Each landform counts once: observations of one event (e.g. the samples of one moraine) are averaged, each group passes through a Huber function (quadratic to 3σ, linear beyond), and the groups are summed, so a satisfied constraint adds nothing instead of diluting the rest. The smoothness prior is summed too (reg_sum=True).

This is the along-centreline grounding-line misfit of Pollard et al. (2016, GMD, "TROUGH") in a mountain valley, with "count each datum once" weights as in Briggs & Tarasov (2013). Overlap scores — the extent sieve of Leger et al. (2025), APCA-type proximity without a sign — go flat when the modelled ice never reaches the margin, the most common failure Ely et al. (2021) report, for the same reason a Jensen–Shannon loss has no gradient between disjoint shapes while a Wasserstein or boundary-distance loss (Arjovsky et al. 2017; Kervadec et al. 2019) does.

7.2 Constant-temperature scans, scored both ways¶

Forward runs at nine constant temperatures (200 m, stake-only climate, archived), scored by the old and the new operators. These are the runs that motivated the switch; the latest inversion is scored both ways in the table above. Old: J2 is flat at 0.3–0.6 from −1 °C up — the inversion could not see La Joux. New: the J2 front is 2.9 km short at +1 °C, 1.8 km at 0 °C, 0.5 km at −1 °C and reached at −1.3 °C, about 1.2 km per °C. On the valley axis Talèfre T1/T2 sit within 35 m of their crests at every temperature from 0 °C up (old misfits 10 and 5, from nunatak ice). The data term (grouped, robust) has its minimum near −1 °C, against +1.0 to +1.6 °C in the first inversion. What still disagrees is Lognan: at the temperature that reaches J2 the modelled surface there is 120–230 m above the moraine crests, which sit at the level of the LIA surface (profile below).

# python tools/run_argentiere_inversion.py --window lg --valley --scan 1 0.5 0 -0.5 -1 -1.5 -2 -2.5 -3
def load_scans(pattern):
    rows, meta = [], {}
    for p in sorted(glob.glob(pattern)):
        with open(p) as f:
            s = json.load(f)
        rows += s["rows"]; meta.update(s["meta"])
    return meta, sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["T"])

# what each temperature is charged, with the grouped robust data term
from core.moraine_obs import huber
def grouped(r, meta):
    g = {}
    for oid, v in r["terms"].items():
        g.setdefault(meta[oid].get("group_id", oid), []).append((meta[oid]["weight"], v))
    return sum(max(w for w, _ in m) * float(huber(torch.tensor(sum(w * v for w, v in m) / sum(w for w, _ in m))))
               for m in g.values())

    print(f"{r['T']:+5.1f}  {grouped(r, meta_new):9.1f}   " + ", ".join(f"{k} {c:.0f}" for c, k in top))

7.3 The speed cap¶

The 300 m/yr cap on depth-averaged speed is reached in the Lognan icefall (the emulator gives 360–400 m/yr there on the mapped LIA geometry). Raising it to 600 m/yr lowers the Argentière surface at Lognan by 30–75 m, and in the Lateglacial scans at −1.0 °C it brings L1 from +121 m to +34 m above its crest and halves the grouped data term (113 → 53). Runs are 1.3–1.8× slower. All later runs use 600 m/yr; section 11 tests 1000 m/yr.

7.4 Gradient check: the first inversion followed a wrong adjoint¶

Before inverting again: do the gradients the optimizer follows match finite differences? Test case: T = −1 °C everywhere, state at 11 ka (2400 years into the lg window), 300 m/yr cap.

quantity at 11 ka adjoint, superbee (first inversion) adjoint, upwind (--adjoint_slope godunov) finite difference
Argentière surface at Lognan, d/dT +452 m/°C −39 m/°C −42 m/°C
… d/dT of the 13.4 ka node alone +201 m/°C 0.0 0.0
Argentière terminus, d/dT −209 m/°C −20 m/°C (native), −675 m/°C (volume surrogate) −968 m/°C
ice volume along the flowline, d/dT — −0.71 km²/°C −1.11 km²/°C
total ice volume, d/dT — −2.9 km³/°C −3.7 km³/°C
  • The superbee-limited transport has an unstable adjoint. Its reported sensitivity grows about twofold per 200 years going back in time; finite differences show the model forgets its state within ~400 years (perturbing the 13.4 ka node by ±0.5 °C changes nothing at 11 ka). Over a 4600-year window the gradient is dominated by the first nodes, and for the Lognan surface it has the wrong sign. The first inversion was fitted with these gradients.
  • Fix: keep superbee in the forward, differentiate the transport as first-order upwind (straight-through, use_adjoint_transport("godunov")). The surface and volume gradients then match finite differences to within 6–36 %, and old nodes get no spurious weight.
  • The terminus needs its own fix. On a grid a glacier advances by filling the next cell, an event the adjoint cannot see, so the native terminus gradient is ~1/50 of the true one. The volume surrogate (volume_scale, value unchanged, gradient through the tongue's thickening) brings it to 0.7×.

7.5 Running, and next¶

results/argentiere_lg_200m_valley/ (started 22 Oct, launch.sh there): the Lateglacial window with the valley operators, grouped robust data term, 600 m/yr cap, upwind adjoint, from T = −1 °C. Open at that point:

  1. Precipitation. The stake-only calibration (section 2) gives 4.7 m/yr; see section 9.
  2. The H ≥ 0 clamp in igm_emulator_step comes before the SMB is added (section 7, top).
  3. Lognan crest elevations come from the bed at the mapped line; the boulder elevations (2189–2287 m) would be tighter.

8. From the first inversion to the latest¶

Four Lateglacial inversions, each fixing what the previous one showed:

run grid climate landform operators gradient best loss
results_archive/argentiere_lg_200m (section 5 originally) 200 m stakes, P 4.7 m/yr, T_present 1.0 °C at the landform's cells, mean superbee adjoint (wrong, 7.4) 0.95 (mean, not comparable)
results/argentiere_lg_200m_valley 200 m stakes along the valleys, grouped upwind, full emulator adjoint (stalled at iteration 5) 43.9
results/argentiere_lg_200m_phys 200 m literature + envelope (section 9) along the valleys, grouped upwind, frozen velocity, capped 25.9
results/argentiere_lg_100m_phys (latest, sections 5, 10, 11) 100 m literature + envelope along the valleys, grouped upwind, frozen velocity, capped 22.7

Why the second run stalled. It ran five iterations (data term 53.0 → 43.9). From iteration 5 every gradient was non-finite; the runner skipped the step, T had not changed, and it repeated the same failure for 33 iterations (13 h).

Cause. The loss, the operators' derivatives and the forward model are finite there. What fails is the adjoint of the ice thickness: re-running the model at an iterate next to the failing one (scratch script nan_hunt.py) shows it growing from 5e-3 at 9.2 ka to 3e24 at 10.2 ka (about 5 %/yr, 0.5 % per time step) while T is constant, so the gradient norm overflows. The growth sits in one cell that holds 6 m of ice at 2,212 m for a thousand years, a thin patch at a steady margin. It comes with the velocity's dependence on thickness: with the velocity held constant within each step (--no_emulator_grad) the same run has an adjoint maximum of 2.5e-2 and a finite gradient, with a backward pass of 6 instead of 11 minutes. At the last good iterate that gradient points the same way as the full one (cosine 0.93) and is 2.7 times larger, which Adam does not mind.

What changed. tools/run_argentiere_inversion.py now backtracks to the best iterate with half the step when a gradient is non-finite, gives up after three failures in a row, and keeps the evidence in nonfinite_<i>.json. New flags: --init_from, --no_emulator_grad, --cfl, --probe_adjoint, --adjoint_clip, --reg_slope. results/argentiere_lg_200m_valley_r2 restarts from the best iterate of the stalled run with --no_emulator_grad.

A CFL number of 0.6 halves the forward time and changes the data term by 3 % and the ice volume by 0.5 %, but shifts the advance and retreat timing of the Argentière terminus by up to 3.5 km at single snapshots, so 0.3 is kept.

9. Physical constraints on precipitation and temperature¶

Why the section-2 calibration had to go. The stakes fix the ELA and the balance gradient, not the precipitation (the T–P trade-off of section 2). Pinning T at 1.0 °C made the stakes ask for 4.7 m/yr of precipitation. Over the 2012 glacier that is 3.2 m w.e./yr of accumulation, while the measured glacier-wide winter balance is 1.47 m w.e. (Pléiades 2012–2020, Davaze et al. 2020). The model was therefore building about twice too much ice in the accumulation area. That is the same bias as the 2012 front 1.8 km too long, an ice surface 50–140 m above the Lateglacial lateral moraines, and buried bedrock samples.

Literature values used (--climate phys, CLIMATES["phys"] in tools/run_argentiere_inversion.py).

quantity value source
precipitation, present 1.8 m/yr (below 2.0) Chamonix 1.28 m/yr at 1,042 m; Col du Dôme accumulation ~2.5 m w.e./yr at 4,250 m (Preunkert et al. 2000)
check: glacier-wide accumulation 1.40 m w.e./yr measured winter balance 1.47 m w.e. (Davaze et al. 2020)
seasonal half-range T_s 9.4 °C Chamonix normals 1981–2010 (January −2.2, July 16.5 °C)
degree-day factor 10 mm w.e. K⁻¹ d⁻¹ (upper bound allowed) ice 5.5 (Réveillet et al. 2017, daily PDD); a monthly PDD with no daily variability needs a larger factor
T at 2,000 m, 2012–2021 −0.89 °C fitted to the glacier-wide balance −0.66 m w.e./yr (Davaze et al. 2020)
past precipitation 7 %/°C (Clausius–Clapeyron) Younger Dryas at −4 °C gives −24 %; Kerschner & Ivy-Ochs: −20 to −30 % in the central Alps, about present on the northwestern fringe

With P below 2 m/yr the stakes and the geodetic balance cannot both be matched. The fit keeps the geodetic balance, because it controls the ice volume, and the stakes then come out at rmse 0.66 m w.e. (0.41 before). The ablation zone melts 0.46 m w.e./yr less than measured. The fitted present temperature is 2 °C below the Chamonix value extrapolated with the lapse rate. It is an effective on-glacier temperature for this scheme, and the temperatures below should be read as anomalies from it.

A precipitation gradient (+2 to +12 %/100 m) improves the stake fit only by bringing back the high-altitude excess: 3–6 m w.e./yr of accumulation at 4,000 m. It is not used.

Temperature envelope (--t_bounds, T_ENVELOPE). Each node is kept inside a range of anomalies from pre-industrial (1871–1900), and the present is taken as pre-industrial + 2.0 °C (MeteoSwiss).

period anomaly from pre-industrial (°C) basis
Allerød, 13.6–12.9 ka −4.0 to +0.5 chironomids, Allerød about 2 °C below the early Holocene (Samartin et al. 2012; Heiri et al. 2015)
Younger Dryas, 12.9–11.7 ka −6.5 to −1.0 Argentière: summers 3.0–5.5 °C below present (Protin et al. 2019); Egesen: summer −3.5 °C (Kerschner & Ivy-Ochs)
Preboreal, 11.7–10.0 ka −4.0 to +1.0 as above, warming into the Holocene
early Holocene, 10–9 ka −2.5 to +1.5 chironomids, up to 1–1.5 °C above pre-industrial

The bounds are wide on purpose. They exclude what the literature excludes and otherwise leave the data free. A node sitting on a bound means the landforms and the literature disagree there.

The previous valley run (argentiere_lg_200m_valley_r2) used P = 4.7 m/yr and was deleted. Section 8 still shows its saved outputs, but re-running it now fails, because those result files no longer exist.

# Present-day mass balance: stake-only calibration (section 2) against the literature-constrained one
from core.climate import apply_lapse_rate, compute_negative_temperature_ratio, compute_integral_positive_temperature
st9 = pd.read_csv("data/Argentiere/sources/present/SMB_argentiere_2012-2021_utm32N.csv")
nc = netCDF4.Dataset("data/Argentiere/argentiere_100m.nc")
bed100 = np.asarray(nc["topg"][:]); t12 = np.asarray(nc["thk_2012"][:]); t21 = np.asarray(nc["thk_2021"][:])
m12 = np.asarray(nc["argentiere_2012"][:]) > 0.5; nc.close()
zs9 = (bed100 + 0.5 * (t12 + t21))[m12]                     # 2012-2021 mean surface of the glacier

def smb_parts(z, c):
    """Accumulation and melt (m w.e./yr) at elevations z for climate c, at its present temperature."""
    Tm = apply_lapse_rate(torch.tensor(np.asarray(z, float)), torch.tensor(c["T_present"], dtype=torch.float64), z_ref=c["z_ref"])
    Ts = torch.tensor(c["T_s"], dtype=torch.float64)
    return ((c["precip"] * compute_negative_temperature_ratio(Tm, Ts)).numpy(),
            (c["melt_factor"] * compute_integral_positive_temperature(Tm, Ts)).numpy())

10. The result in brief¶

  • Run: results/argentiere_lg_100m_phys: 100 m grid, literature climate, literature envelope, valley-referenced landform scoring; 30 iterations, loss 23.66 → 22.74 (section 5).
  • Temperature at 2000 m: −5.54 °C on average in the Younger Dryas (12.9–11.7 ka), i.e. 4.65 °C below 2012–2021, 2.65 °C below pre-industrial. The coldest node is −5.65 °C at 12.2 ka. It stays near −5.1 to −5.4 °C until 10.2 ka, then warms to −2.41 °C at 9.0 ka. No node touches the literature envelope. Protin et al. (2019) give Younger Dryas / early-Holocene summers 3.0–5.5 °C below present for the same moraines.
  • Fit: J2 (La Joux frontal), Lognan L2 and the Talèfre laterals are met. The valley-side ice at La Joux and Lognan is 55–80 m above the lateral crests, and 4 of 17 bedrock samples are under 46–149 m of ice. That is a glacier too thick for its length, which one temperature cannot fix (section 6).
  • Compared with the earlier runs (section 8): the summed misfit of the dated moraines fell from 417 (first inversion) to 31.5 (valley operators), 17.6 (literature climate, 200 m) and 13.6 (100 m).
  • Uncertainty: section 11.
  • Video: results/argentiere_lg_100m_phys/video/argentiere_lateglacial_100m.mp4.

11. Sensitivity: what the fixed parameters do to the temperature¶

The inversion fixes everything but T(t). Each fixed number is uncertain, and each one changes the temperature that fits the landforms. tools/sensitivity_argentiere.py measures this one parameter at a time, starting from the 100 m result T*(t):

  1. Perturb one parameter (table below). The mass-balance parameters are calibrated together with the present-day temperature on the geodetic 2012–2021 balance (−0.66 m w.e./yr), so for those the present temperature is re-fitted first, as the calibration would have done (dT_present).
  2. Find the compensating shift. Run the forward model at T*(t) + dT for three (or more) uniform shifts around a first guess and put a parabola through the loss. Its vertex is the shift that makes the perturbed model fit the landforms again. The first guess is the shift that keeps the glacier-wide balance of the modelled Younger Dryas glacier unchanged (mass balance only, no ice flow).
  3. Read it as an anomaly. What carries over to the paleoclimate is the change of the anomaly to the present, dT − dT_present.

The approximation is that the compensation is a uniform shift: a full re-inversion per parameter (~17 h at 100 m) would also let the shape of T(t) change.

parameter base tested basis present T re-fitted
present precipitation 1.8 m/yr 1.5, 2.1 ±17 %: Chamonix 1.28 m/yr at 1042 m, Col du Dôme ~2.5 m w.e. at 4250 m yes
degree-day factor 10 mm/K/d 8, 12 ±20 %; monthly PDD without daily variability yes
seasonal half-range T_s 9.4 °C 7.9, 10.9 ±1.5 °C around Chamonix 1981–2010 yes
lapse rate 7 °C/km 6, 8 usual Alpine range yes
Lateglacial precipitation, relative to the Clausius–Clapeyron scaling ×1 ×0.75, ×1.25 Kerschner & Ivy-Ochs: −20 to −30 % in the central Alps, about present on the NW fringe no
Glen flow-law factor A 78 MPa⁻³/yr 52, 117 ÷1.5, ×1.5, inside the emulator's training range no
sliding, tau_ref 0.2154 MPa 0.15 more sliding; higher values are outside the emulator's training range no
speed cap 600 m/yr 1000 m/yr numerical (section 7.3) no

Data-only uncertainty. The block_* cases shift only the nodes of one period (Allerød 13.6–12.9, Younger Dryas 12.9–11.7, Preboreal 11.7–10.0, early Holocene 10.0–9.0 ka) with the base parameters. The loss is a sum of σ-normalized squared residuals (Huber beyond 3σ), about −2 × log-likelihood, so its curvature L″ gives σ = √(2 / L″). With the other periods held fixed this is a lower bound.

          ("Ppaleo", "Lateglacial precipitation"), ("A", "flow-law factor A"), ("tau", "sliding tau_ref"), ("cap", "speed cap")]
